chapter_theme: The அல்ல ten denies a thing its name when one inner condition is missing: a spouse who does not know the other's nature, a house without an excellent wife, kin without tenderness, a friend without consent, learning without submission, giving off aram's road, penance not rightly undertaken, and age that does not know rebirth.

41.reading: One who does not conduct himself with knowledge of the other's nature is said not to be a spouse.
41.nuance: தாரம் ordinarily names a wife, yet the participle and predicate are masculine (ஒழுகாதான், அல்லன்). Either the line, as written, applies the word for a spouse to the husband who does not know his wife's nature, or the masculine endings stand for an older feminine reading (the woman who does not act knowing her husband's nature is no wife). The masculine reading is followed here because it is what the text has. நீர், 'nature', names whose nature only by context. Line 1 is the frame line of the ten.

norm.note: a rule of the period on what makes a spouse: conduct fitted to the partner's nature; if the line is read as feminine it is a rule for a wife's conduct

items.claim: one who acts without knowing the other's nature is not a true spouse

42.reading: A household life whose wife is not excellent is said not to be a household life at all.
42.nuance: The saying puts the whole worth of வாழ்க்கை, the life of the house, on the wife's மாண்பு; it says nothing of the husband here, though the line before it, read as written, set a condition on him.

norm.note: a norm of the period that measures the household by the wife's excellence

items.claim: a household whose wife lacks excellence is no real household life

43.reading: Kin-friendship that has no moistness of heart is said not to be kin-friendship.
43.nuance: கிளைநட்பு joins the kin-group (கிளை) and friendship (நட்பு): the saying holds that relation by blood does not by itself make the bond; ஈரம், wetness, the tenderness of heart, does. ஈரலில் is taken as ஈரம் இல் with an unusual spelling; ஈரல் by itself would be the liver.

items.claim: a tie with kin that lacks tenderness is not truly a bond of kin

44.reading: A man whose hand never loosens to give is said not to be one whose name stands high like a mountain.
44.nuance: சோராக் கை is a hand that does not slacken or let go, taken here as the closed hand of the miser, since the ten names defective things. சொன்மலை is read as சொல் + மலை, 'a mountain of word', i.e. great renown; it could also mean one whose word stands firm like a mountain, which would make the saying about the miser's promises. Either way the closed hand forfeits a standing of the word.

items.claim: the tight-fisted man is not one whose renown is great

45.reading: One whose heart does not agree with one is said not to be a friend.
45.nuance: நேர்தல் is to agree, consent, come straight; நேரா நெஞ்சம் is a heart that has not come into accord, whatever the outward dealings. The verb returns in 46 and, as நேர்லா, in 49, so three sayings in the ten turn on consent or undertaking.

items.claim: one whose heart does not consent to the bond is no friend

46.reading: What is learnt without submitting or consenting to the learning is said not to be learning.
46.nuance: நேராமல் may mean without the heart's assent, without submitting to the teacher, or without the formal undertaking (or fee) by which a pupil is accepted. All three make learning depend on a relation entered into, not on the content gained; the line does not fix which.

items.claim: learning taken in without assent or submission is not real learning

47.reading: Strain endured without coming to live well by it is said not to count as strain.
47.nuance: வருத்தம் here is taken as the labour of effort, measured by whether one comes to live (வாழ்தல்) by it. A second reading is open: grief suffered by one who has not lived rightly is not true suffering, i.e. it is deserved. The line does not decide between them.

items.claim: toil that does not bring one to thrive is not reckoned as real effort

48.reading: What is not given along the way of aram is said not to be giving.
48.nuance: ஈனை is read as giving (ஈதல், ஈகை). The test is not the size of the gift but the road it travels, அறத்தாறு; the saying does not say what that road requires. The bracketed (து) is an editorial supply.

items.claim: a gift not made along the path of dharma is not true giving

49.reading: What is not undertaken in the proper manner is said not to be a vow of penance.
49.nuance: நோன்பு is a vow or observance of restraint. The line is built as a twin of 48: அறத்தாற்றின் / திறத்தாற்றின், giving judged by aram's road, penance by its own proper road (திறம்). நேர்லா is read as a form of நேர்தல், to undertake, so the penance is defined by the manner in which it is entered on.

items.claim: an observance not taken up in its proper way is no true penance

50.reading: Age that does not know of the birth to come is said not to be true old age.
50.nuance: மூப்பு is ordinarily just age; the saying makes it a state reached by knowing, not by years. மறுபிறப்பு assumes rebirth as a thing to be known. The ten ends where 39 in the previous ten also judged old age, there by its disgrace, here by its ignorance.

items.claim: an old age that has no awareness of rebirth is not real elderhood

links.note: 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature; 42 denies the name of household life to a house whose wife is not excellent.
links.teaches: Read as written, the ten opens with a condition on the husband before it measures the house by the wife, so the household is made to fail from either side and not from the wife alone.

links.note: Thirikadugam 96 names the wife who knows her husband's hint as one at whose word rain falls; saying 41 denies the name of spouse to one who does not act knowing the other's nature.
links.teaches: The same virtue, knowing the partner's nature, is a power over the rains in one work and the bare minimum of being a spouse in the other, so it is both the ceiling and the floor of marriage.

links.note: Kural 52 says that if the wife lacks household excellence the life is nothing whatever else it has; saying 42 says the same in the அல்ல form.
links.teaches: The Kural's claim that a wife's excellence decides the household survives the move into a book of bare definitions, where it becomes one of the tests by which a thing earns its name.
links.list_adds: It sets household life beside kin-friendship, giving, learning and penance as things that lose their very name when one inner condition fails, so the wife's excellence becomes a defining condition of the same kind as aram in giving.

links.note: Naladiyar 56 says that even a wife without good qualities cannot be put away, and that this is why marriage is called கடி; saying 42 says a house whose wife is not excellent is no household life.
links.teaches: Put together, the two say that the life which the saying denies the name of household is one the man still cannot leave, so 'not a life' names a bond that persists as a hardship.
links.list_adds: Its list denies such a house the name of a life outright, where the quatrain keeps the marriage and counts its cost.

links.note: Saying 11 says birth into a great house is known by ஈரம; saying 43 says kin-friendship without ஈரம் is no kin-friendship.
links.teaches: The book uses the same moistness of heart twice, as the sign of good birth and as the condition of kin's bond, so blood and lineage are both made to depend on a tenderness that birth alone does not give.

links.note: Kural 522 says kin whose love does not lapse bring ever-branching gains; saying 43 says a kin bond without tenderness is not a kin bond.
links.teaches: The Kural values kin by the gains their unfailing love brings, while the saying moves the test inward and denies the name of kin to those without tenderness, before any gain is counted.
links.list_adds: It puts the kin bond in a run of definitions by inner condition (spouse, house, friend, learning), so kinship is ranked with friendship as a bond made by feeling, where the couplet treats kin as a source of wealth.

links.note: Kural 231 says giving and living with renown is the only gain of life; saying 44 says the man whose hand never loosens is no mountain of renown.
links.teaches: The Kural joins giving and fame as the one profit of living; the saying shows the same bond from its failure, that the closed hand loses the standing of one's name, on the reading of சொன்மலை as renown.
links.list_adds: It states the bond negatively and puts the miser among other false holders of a name (the unfeeling kinsman, the friend whose heart does not consent), a contrast of claim and substance the couplet lacks.

links.note: Kural 786 says friendship that smiles in the face is not friendship and friendship that smiles in the heart is; saying 45 says one whose heart does not agree is no friend.
links.teaches: Both deny the name of friendship by the same 'is not' form, and the saying narrows the Kural's heart-smile to consent, so the friend is one whose heart has come into agreement, not only one who feels warmth.
links.list_adds: It sets the false friend beside the false spouse, kinsman, learning, giving and penance, so the Kural's one test for friendship becomes a general method: each bond or practice is named by an inner condition.

links.note: Both sayings turn on நேர்தல்: the friend whose heart does not agree, the learning gained without consent or submission.
links.teaches: Placed side by side, the two make friendship and learning both depend on an act of assent, so the pupil's submission to learning is the same act as the friend's agreement of heart.

links.note: Kural 395 praises those who learned yearning before the learned like the poor before the rich; saying 46 says learning without நேர்தல் is not learning.
links.teaches: The Kural ranks the humble learner highest; the saying goes further and denies that learning without that assent or submission is learning at all, on the reading of நேராமல் as not submitting.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's ranking into a definition and puts learning beside friendship and penance as things that exist only when entered into by consent or undertaking.

links.note: Saying 8 ranks serving the learned above learning; saying 46 denies the name of learning to what is learnt without submission.
links.teaches: Across two tens, the book first puts reverence for teachers above learning and then makes it the condition of learning, so reverence moves from the greater good to the thing without which learning does not exist.

links.note: Kural 619 says that even where fate denies the end, effort pays the wage of bodily strain; saying 47 says strain that does not bring one to live is not strain, on the reading of வருத்தம் as effort.
links.teaches: The Kural promises effort a wage even in failure, while the saying refuses to count strain that brings no living, so the pair sets a floor (some wage) against a definition by result (a life gained).
links.list_adds: It names effort among things judged by an outcome or manner beside giving and penance, a measure by result the couplet explicitly sets aside.

links.note: Kural 221 says giving to those who have nothing is giving and all else is a measured return; saying 48 says what is not given in aram's way is not giving.
links.teaches: Both redefine giving by denying the name to gifts that look like it; the Kural fixes the test by recipient and expected return, while the saying fixes it by the road of aram and leaves its content open.
links.list_adds: It pairs the test of giving with a matching test of penance in the next line (அறத்தாற்றின் / திறத்தாற்றின்), so the householder's gift and the ascetic's vow are judged by one rule of right manner, which the couplet does not do.

links.note: Saying 34 reckons giving without care for the receiver no better than refusing; saying 48 says giving not along aram's way is not giving.
links.teaches: The book judges giving twice by its manner, once by care for the receiver and once by aram's road, so a gift's worth never rests on its size in either ten.

links.note: The two lines are built as twins: அறத்தாற்றின் ஈயாதது ஈனையன்று, திறத்தாற்றின் நேர்லாதது நோன்பன்று.
links.teaches: The twin form makes the giver's gift and the ascetic's vow two cases of one rule, that an act is named by the way it is done, so the householder's and renouncer's codes are tested alike.

links.note: Kural 261 defines தவம் as bearing pain and harming no living being; saying 49 says a vow not taken up in its proper way is no penance.
links.teaches: The Kural defines penance by its content, endurance and harmlessness, while the saying defines it by how it is undertaken, so the pair shows two separate tests a vow must pass.
links.list_adds: It sets penance as the twin of giving in a matched pair of lines, putting the ascetic's vow under the same test of right manner as the householder's gift, which the couplet does not.

links.note: Thirikadugam 96 names the ascetic who carries out what he has undertaken in the proper way as one at whose word rain falls; saying 49 says a vow not undertaken in its proper way is no penance.
links.teaches: One work denies the name of penance to a vow wrongly undertaken; the other promises rain to the ascetic who completes his vow rightly, so between them the proper manner is both the condition of penance and the source of its power.

links.note: Purananuru 195 tells grey-haired elders in useless age that Death will bind them and urges them at least to refrain from harm; saying 50 says age without knowledge of the next birth is not old age.
links.teaches: The puram poet shames old men by the coming of Death, while the saying denies them the name of age unless they know what follows death, so the heroic warning about the end becomes a doctrine of rebirth.

links.note: Saying 39 reckons disgraced old age no better than anger; saying 50 says age that does not know rebirth is not old age.
links.teaches: The book judges old age twice and never by years: once by the disgrace it carries, once by what it knows of the birth to come, so elderhood is a moral and a spiritual standing.

source_issues: show flags saying 41 as site_diff: the online text lacks line 2 (நீரறிந்து ஒழுகாதான் தாரம் அல்லன்); line 1 is the frame line repeated at the head of each ten.
Saying 41 pairs தாரம், ordinarily 'wife', with masculine ஒழுகாதான் and அல்லன்; this may be a scribal or editorial masculinisation of a line about a wife.
Saying 42 (தார(ம்)மா ணாதது) and 48 (ஈயாத(து)) carry bracketed editorial supplies.
Saying 43 has ஈரலில், taken as ஈரம் இல் (ஈரல் alone is 'liver').
Sayings 49 and 50 are spaced across word boundaries (நேர்லா ததுநோன் பன்று; மறுபிறப் பறியா ததுமூப் பன்று); நேர்லாதது is an unusual form of நேர்தல்.
